newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/mark up at U.S. noon, eyes Chirac, Kok remarks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark up at U.S. noon, eyes Chirac, Kok remarks.

text.p: The dollar hovered near session highs at midday, aided by upbeat remarks from French President Jacques Chirac and Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok about a meeting to be held next week in Amsterdam, currency experts said.

Speaking one day after the French Socialist-led government asked for a delay to study the European Union (EU) stability pact, Chirac said he hoped an agreement on the pact could be reached at the summit.
Chirac also reiterated France's committment to launch the euro in January 1999 as planned.
Kok added to the positive sentiment by saying he hoped it would be possible to have "good preparations" on the stability pact before the summit, but he added "there is no guarantee."
The comments by Chirac and Kok probably helped "boost it a little," said Cynthia Cooley, a foreign exchange analyst and trader at United Gulf Bank of Bahrain in Boston.
Cooley noted there was very little activity in the market.
In a market like this, traders will "grab for any news and the news that came out happened to be more or less dollar supportive," she added.
The dollar climbed to 1.7180/90 marks at noon from 1.7125/35 at the open. It briefly hit 1.7210 marks shortly after midday.
The German currency also lost ground to the Swiss franc, trading near 0.8393/98 francs after midday compared to around 0.8420/21 francs in early morning dealings.
Experts attributed some of the strength in dollar/mark to the pullback in mark/Swiss.
MCM CurrencyWatch international economist Kevin Harris pointed out that this is the first day in three weeks that the Swiss National Bank did not add liquidity overnight.
Harris also noted that some dollar gains reflected short covering as European players prepared to go home.
Elsewhere, the greenback remained mired in a tight range against the yen, changing hands at 112.35/40 at midday compared with 112.45/50 at the open.

Market players are awaiting the release of Japan's current account surplus at 2350 GMT on Tuesday. Economists polled by Reuters, on average, predicted the surplus in April grew to 1.13 trillion yen, up sharply from 566.6 billion yen last year.
For his part, Keisuke Aso, manager of the forex service department at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, doubted the current account data would have a significant impact.
Still Aso warned there are lots of potential sellers on any rebound in the dollar, including Japanese exporters and foreign investors who need to hedge their positions.
A flurry of potentially market moving U.S. economic figures for May are also due out this week, beginning with retail sales on Thursday and the producer prices index (PPI) on Friday.
David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics, said market players are waiting to gauge the prospects for a Federal Reserve tightening based on the U.S. data.
Fed policymakers next meet on July 1 and 2 to decide whether to hike short-term interest rates again. The central bank increased the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent in March.
In other trading, the dollar fetched 1.4428/38 Swiss francs, up from 1.4415/25 at the open.
Sterling was litttle changed at $1.6380/85 compared with $1.6383/93.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3858/63 from C$1.3865/70.
